{"id": "a32c98e5-7bd9-443e-a5c6-08035d8980af", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_hYOUiL7Oj7PePhsTFaZHfh", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"AWS PrivateLink for Amazon S3\",\"context\":\"## Types of VPC endpoints for Amazon S3\\n\\nYou can use two types of VPC endpoints to access Amazon S3: *gateway\\nendpoints* and *interface endpoints* (by using AWS PrivateLink).\\nA *gateway endpoint* is a gateway that you specify in your\\nroute table to access Amazon S3 from your VPC over the AWS network. *Interface endpoints* extend the functionality of gateway endpoints by using\\nprivate IP addresses to route requests to Amazon S3 from within your VPC, on premises, or from a\\nVPC in another AWS Region by using VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway. If you have an existing gateway\\nendpoint in the VPC, you can use both types of endpoints in the same VPC.\\n\\n| Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3 | Interface endpoints for Amazon S3 |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| In both cases, your network traffic remains on the AWS network. | |\\n| Use Amazon S3 public IP addresses | Use private IP addresses from your VPC to access Amazon S3 |\\n| Use the same Amazon S3 DNS names | Require endpoint-specific Amazon S3 DNS names |\\n| Do not allow access from on premises | Allow access from on premises |\\n| Do not allow access from another AWS Region | Allow access from a VPC in another AWS Region by using VPC peering or AWS Transit Gateway |\\n| Not billed | Billed |\\n\\nFor more information, see Gateway endpoints and interface VPC endpoints in the\\n*AWS PrivateLink Guide*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/privatelink-interface-endpoints.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Gateway endpoints for Amazon S3\",\"context\":\"## Considerations\\n\\n* A gateway endpoint is available only in the Region where you created it. Be sure\\n to create your gateway endpoint in the same Region as your S3 buckets.\\n* If you're using the Amazon DNS servers, you must enable both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution\\n for your VPC. If you're using your own DNS server, ensure that requests to Amazon S3\\n resolve correctly to the IP addresses maintained by AWS.\\n* The rules for the security groups for your instances that access Amazon S3 through a\\n gateway endpoint must allow traffic to and from Amazon S3. If so, ensure that your\\n endpoint policy allows the AWS service or resource to access these buckets using the\\n `s3:GetObject` action.\\n* You can't use the `aws:SourceIp` condition in an identity policy or\\n a bucket policy for requests to Amazon S3 that traverse a VPC endpoint. Instead, use the\\n `aws:VpcSourceIp` condition. The following example creates an interface endpoint to Amazon S3 in `us-west-2` from a VPC in `us-east-1`.\\n\\n```\\naws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint \\\\\\n --vpc-id vpc-id \\\\\\n --service-name com.amazonaws.us-west-2.s3 \\\\\\n --vpc-endpoint-type Interface \\\\\\n --subnet-ids subnet-id-1 subnet-id-2 \\\\\\n --region us-east-1 \\\\\\n --service-region us-west-2\\n\\n```\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/aws-services-cross-region-privatelink-support.html\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Verify whether S3 VPC interface endpoints support cross-region access"}

For a list of all possible service states, see AWS PrivateLink concepts.\\n* Data processing charges apply for each GB processed through the VPC endpoint, regardless of the traffic's source or destination.\\n\\nFor more information, see AWS PrivateLink pricing\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/integrate-third-party-services/architecture-1.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Understand estimated and actual costs for Deadline Cloud\",\"context\":\"### PrivateLink costs\\n\\nTwo optional Deadline Cloud configurations create VPC\\nendpoints in your account. {"id": "7be6d8ae-3eef-4ea4-bf68-327255c0f468", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "I now have enough to answer: S3 interface endpoints bill per hour per AZ plus per GB processed, and cross-region PrivateLink to S3 is supported via create-vpc-endpoint with a service-region parameter. Importantly, this doesn't eliminate inter-region data transfer costs—it just routes traffic over the AWS backbone instead of through a NAT gateway.

Standard inter-region data transfer pricing still applies regardless of whether you use NAT, an internet gateway, or cross-region PrivateLink, since AWS charges based on the egress region. However, NAT Gateway's per-GB data processing fee (around $0.045/GB) is typically pricier than the interface endpoint's processing fee (roughly $0.01/GB plus hourly per-AZ charges), so for large volumes, PrivateLink can still mean real savings—it's a cost swap on the processing fee, not an elimination of transfer charges.

Gateway endpoints aren't an option here since they're region-locked, making interface endpoints the only cross-region path. The truly optimal fix would be avoiding cross-region reads entirely—via replication or co-locating compute with the data—since that eliminates both NAT fees and inter-region transfer costs; short of that, the interface endpoint is the practical recommendation.

Running the numbers at 5,000 GB/month: NAT Gateway processing alone would run roughly $225/month plus ~$33 hourly charge, while an Interface Endpoint would cost around $50 in processing plus $15-22 hourly across AZs — totaling $65-72/month, a savings of over $150/month before even counting inter-region transfer fees that apply either way.

But I shouldn't rely on memorized pricing figures since AWS pricing varies by region and can change over time — I need to verify these NAT Gateway and PrivateLink numbers before presenting them as fact, so I'll use verify_aws_claim to confirm current rates.

"}]}

{"id": "9dda70fb-cb08-4cd4-86b5-c5132f8116f3", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "A Cross-Region Interface Endpoint for S3 is technically possible — AWS added cross-region PrivateLink support, so you can create an interface endpoint in your VPC's region that targets S3 in a different region (e.g. `--service-name com.amazonaws.us-west-2.s3 --service-region us-west-2` from a VPC in `us-east-1`). But it's a partial fix, not a complete one — here's the cost math:

**What it saves:** NAT Gateway charges a $0.045/GB data processing fee on top of data transfer. At 5,000 GB/month, that's **~$225/month** in NAT processing fees alone that would move off the NAT Gateway path.

**What it doesn't save:**
- **Inter-region data transfer charges still apply.** Those are billed on the transfer itself (egress from the bucket's region), regardless of whether the traffic goes through a NAT Gateway, an internet gateway, or a PrivateLink interface endpoint. Routing through an Interface Endpoint doesn't make the read "same-region" — it just changes the on-ramp.
- **New costs:** Interface endpoints bill hourly per AZ plus their own per-GB data processing fee, so you're not eliminating a charge, you're swapping one data-path's processing fee for a (likely smaller) one.
- You'll want to size this against your actual AZ count and traffic pattern to confirm it nets out positive — it almost always will for 5,000 GB/month, but worth confirming with real numbers.

**The bigger question:** why is this read pattern cross-region at all? If it's recurring/predictable, the more complete fix is usually to eliminate the cross-region hop entirely — e.g., S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in the compute's region, a CloudFront/cache layer, or relocating the workload closer to the data. That removes both the NAT fee *and* the inter-region transfer fee, instead of just the NAT fee.

Want me to pull the actual flow log data and bucket/VPC regions to run a precise cost comparison between the interface endpoint and a same-region replication approach?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
